findings.problem: The section teaches that a 14-hour intern shift is lawful work of which only 12 hours are creditable. orientation[2] says 'a longer shift can be worked', the worked example's resolution calls the 14 hours 'time lawfully worked under supervision', and common_traps[2] treats a supervised 14-hour shift as a credit question only. Massachusetts separately bars a pharmacy intern (and a pharmacist) from practising in a pharmacy for more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period without an eight-consecutive-hour rest period; the only relief is an extenuating circumstance, acted on in the patient's best interest, with the excess minimized and documented by the licensee.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.01(17) names pharmacy interns expressly. The scenario states no extenuating circumstance, so on its own facts both the intern and the preceptor who was 'present throughout' exceeded the limit. Learning objective 2 (time at a site versus creditable hours) is therefore taught on a false premise, and the error compounds with the section's own teaching that an intern's violation of state regulations may bar the licensure examination under 247 CMR 8.01(17). The 12-hour credit ceiling in 247 CMR 8.01(4) is stated correctly; what is wrong is the proposition that the uncredited hours were lawfully worked.

findings.problem: The only daily time limit the section gives is the 12-hour credit ceiling, and its stated consequence ('Time worked beyond that in the same day does not reach the internship requirement') presupposes that the extra time may be worked. The practice limit of 12 hours in any 24-hour period, with a mandatory eight-consecutive-hour rest period, is absent.
findings.rationale: Two different 12-hour numbers apply to a Massachusetts intern and they are measured against different things: 247 CMR 8.01(4) against internship credit per day, and 247 CMR 9.01(17) against time practising in a pharmacy in any 24-hour period. A candidate taught only the first will answer a long-shift question on credit alone.

findings.problem: The rule for recording a day's hours sends any time beyond 12 hours straight to bookkeeping ('record any additional time worked as something other than internship credit') without first testing whether practising that long was permitted at all.
findings.rationale: Under 247 CMR 9.01(17) more than 12 hours of practice in 24 requires an extenuating circumstance, minimisation of the excess and documentation by the licensee, and is otherwise a violation. The condition-to-action rule should check the practice limit before it reaches the credit record.

findings.problem: Learning objective 2 promises to identify who may directly supervise a pharmacy intern, but the section answers only with the title 'registered pharmacist preceptor' and never conveys what that defined term requires or what direct supervision consists of. Under 247 CMR 2.00 a preceptor is a registered pharmacist in good standing, with at least one year of actual practice, whom the Board has approved to supervise and direct the training of pharmacy interns; and direct supervision of an intern is the supervision a Board-approved registered pharmacist preceptor gives by overseeing and directing the intern's professional activities, including directly reviewing the intern's work.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 8.01(3) turns on two defined terms. Without the definitions a candidate cannot tell that a newly licensed pharmacist, a pharmacist not in good standing, or one the Board has not approved may not act as preceptor, or that presence alone is not the whole of direct supervision. Preceptor eligibility is a natural examination fact pattern for exactly the objective the section declares.

findings.problem: The entry-route table describes the candidate as any 'Graduate of an approved college or school of pharmacy, not yet licensed' and says 'Nothing further' is required. 247 CMR 8.01(10) is narrower: it lets 'a pharmacy intern who has graduated' continue to act as a pharmacy intern until licensed.
findings.rationale: 8.01(10) preserves an existing intern's capacity through graduation; it does not confer intern status on a graduate who never held a Massachusetts intern license, and 8.01(2) conditions intern-license eligibility on first-professional-year standing and current PharmD enrolment. orientation[3] and exceptions[3] correctly say 'continue', but the table cell drops the precondition.

findings.problem: The 8.01(9) reporting duty is framed as triggered by 'A Board request for information about the internship'. The regulation imposes it during the course of the internship: preceptors and interns shall in a timely manner submit, on a Board form, such information as the Board may require.
findings.rationale: The duty runs throughout the internship on the Board's standing requirements, not only in response to an ad hoc request; orientation[4] and forms_records[0] state it correctly, so the timing entry is inconsistent with them.

findings.problem: The examination-bar teaching under 8.01(17) is given without the limit the same chapter now contains: 247 CMR 8.08 provides that no person shall be denied initial licensure or renewal because of a complaint, criminal charge, conviction, judgment, discipline or other sanction arising from providing, assisting in providing, or dispensing medication for reproductive or gender-affirming health care services that would have been lawful in Massachusetts and consistent with good professional practice here.
findings.rationale: 8.08 (effective 1/9/25) qualifies the licensure consequences of sanctioned conduct across 247 CMR 8.00, including an intern's route to licensure through the examination. The case is narrow, but the section presents the conduct consequence as unqualified.

results.summary: Every subsection of 247 CMR 8.01 that the section cites is paraphrased accurately: the 1500/1000/500 composition and the ACPE experiential alternative, the 12-hour daily credit ceiling, direct preceptor supervision, the two-intern preceptor cap, intern supervision of technicians, the FPGEE authorization issued within the preceding year, the residency credential, graduation continuation, the 14-day withdrawal notice, and the discretionary, additional examination bar. All ten mapped practice questions are answerable and none is contradicted. The section is not publishable as it stands. HIGH: learning objective 2 is built on the premise that a 14-hour intern shift is lawful and only a credit problem, which 247 CMR 9.01(17) contradicts (no more than 12 hours of practice in 24 without an eight-hour rest, save a documented extenuating circumstance); the same gap runs through timing_deadlines[2] and decision_logic[0]. MEDIUM: the supervising preceptor is named without the 247 CMR 2.00 content (good standing, one year of practice, Board approval; oversight including direct review of the intern's work). LOW: the graduate entry row is broader than 8.01(10), the 8.01(9) duty is framed as request-triggered, and the 8.08 limit is not noted. Targeted edits to about a dozen fields, including rebuilding worked_examples[0], will cure it; a fresh audit is required.

findings.problem: The section states that '247 CMR 8.00 permits support personnel to perform only the duties it names' and limits the pharmacy technician to 'the duties 247 CMR 8.02 names'. 247 CMR 8.00 does not enumerate a technician's permitted technical work: 8.02(6) contains a name-tag duty, two communication permissions (relaying the offer to counsel; unchanged refill authorizations with the pharmacist's approval) and a closed list of prohibited functions.
findings.rationale: Under 247 CMR 2.00 a pharmacy technician, like a trainee, 'performs pharmacy duties under the direct supervision of a pharmacist'; 8.06(1)(b) requires the pharmacy's own written description of the duties delegated to technicians; 8.06(3)(a) counts technicians used to assist in filling prescriptions; and 9.19(17)(c) refers to technical staff performing non-discretionary duties. The scheme is delegation under direct supervision bounded by express prohibitions and conditions, not a closed list of named permissions. Read as written, the section would exclude routine data entry, counting, labeling and staging.

authorities.exact_section: 247 CMR 2.00, definitions of 'Pharmacy Technician' and 'Pharmacy Technician Trainee'

findings.problem: The first decision rule tells the candidate to 'ask whether 247 CMR 8.00 names the task as a permitted duty for that tier; an unnamed duty is not available merely because a pharmacist is willing to supervise it.'
findings.rationale: Because 247 CMR 8.00 names almost no affirmative technician tasks, this test returns the wrong answer for most ordinary technical work a pharmacist may delegate under direct supervision. The correct test is whether the task is delegated technical work, falls outside the prohibited list in 8.02(6)(d) and 8.04(4)(e), and meets any tier-specific condition (8.02(6)(c), 8.03(4)(c), 8.04(4)(c)-(d), 9.04(8)).

findings.location: practice_question_ids[0] (MA-Q-0075), read against decision_logic[0].action and orientation[0].text
findings.problem: MA-Q-0075 keys as correct that a trainee under direct supervision may collect and enter nonclinical demographic information (A), perform authorised prescription-processing and staging tasks (C) and continue other clerical or technical functions (D). None of those tasks is named in 247 CMR 8.00, so the section's named-duty test marks them unavailable and contradicts the key on at least option A.
findings.rationale: A mapped practice question must be answerable from the section and not contradicted by it. Here the section's own decision rule points a candidate away from the keyed answer, while the key is consistent with the 247 CMR 2.00 definition and 8.03(4)(b).

findings.problem: Vaccine and medication administration is presented as closed to every technician tier 'however the pharmacy has written its protocols', and ma_vs_federal is empty. The federal PREP Act COVID-19 Declaration, as amended by the 12th Amendment (89 FR 99875, Dec. 11, 2024), extends coverage through December 31, 2029 for qualified pharmacy technicians to administer COVID-19 vaccines (age three and older), seasonal influenza vaccines (age 19 and older) and specified COVID-19 therapeutics. Conditions include a supervising pharmacist readily and immediately available, ACPE-approved practical training and current CPR certification, and the Declaration treats contrary State law as preempted.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 8.02(6)(d) and 8.04(4)(e) are stated correctly as Massachusetts regulation, but on Massachusetts facts in 2026 the categorical retrieval answer is wrong for these covered countermeasures. A Federal Register search found no later amendment to the Declaration through the audit date. The section should give the Massachusetts prohibition together with the federal PREP Act overlay, its conditions and its sunset.

findings.problem: The eligibility requirements (good moral character; no drug-related felony conviction or admission to sufficient facts) and renewal are taught as applying to every applicant without the exception in 247 CMR 8.08: no person may be denied initial licensure or renewal because of a complaint, charge, conviction, judgment, discipline or other sanction arising from providing, assisting in providing, or dispensing medication for reproductive or gender-affirming health care services that would have been lawful in Massachusetts.
findings.rationale: 8.08 (effective 1/9/25) sits in the same chapter and directly qualifies the entry and renewal rules the section declares as its scope. Narrow, but an express exception.

findings.problem: Two cells state contestable readings as settled law. (1) The trainee is said to be barred from requesting and accepting refill authorizations by telephone 'for the same reason' as the carve-out, but 8.03(4)(c) bars trainees from taking 'prescriptions' over the telephone, and the regulations treat 'authorizations for refills' (8.02(6)(c)) and 'new prescriptions over the telephone' (9.04(8)) as distinct. (2) The certified technician is said to get no relief from the unchanged-information condition, but 8.04(4)(c) attaches no such condition to a certified technician's refill requests and lets the certified technician, with the pharmacist's approval, receive new prescription information, as 9.04(8) also allows.
findings.rationale: The conclusions may be defensible, but the section should either support them or mark them as interpretation; as written they overstate the text, and cell (2) sits in tension with 9.04(8).

findings.problem: Direct supervision is presented as the trainee's distinguishing condition ('Yes, but only while acting under the direct supervision of a pharmacist'), while the licensed technician's row and quick_review[10] speak only of unspecified 'pharmacist supervision'. 247 CMR 2.00 defines the pharmacy technician, like the trainee, as performing pharmacy duties under the direct supervision of a pharmacist, and defines the direct supervision a pharmacist must give a pharmacy technician.
findings.rationale: The contrast invites the inference that a licensed technician needs only general supervision, which the definitions do not support.

findings.problem: The program check tests a training program only against the 8.02(4) categories and the 120/120-hour split. On the examination route, 8.02(3)(e)3.a also requires the Board-approved training program to cover specified topics: job descriptions, pharmacy security, commonly used medical abbreviations, routes of administration, product selection, final check by pharmacists, guidelines for the use of pharmacy technicians, and any other Board requirements.
findings.rationale: Learning objective 3 covers which training programs the Board recognises; the required topic coverage is part of that test and appears nowhere in the section.

results.summary: Entry, trainee limits, examination content, certification lapse and licence renewal under 247 CMR 8.02-8.04 and 8.07 are paraphrased accurately, and every number checks: 16 and 18 years, 1500 hours or one year whichever is shorter with its three exceptions, 30 days after the 18th birthday, 120/120 hours, 500 attested trainee hours, the six examination areas, two-year birthdate expiry, and the more-than-two-year lapse. Three Medium defects prevent release. First, the section recasts technician scope as a closed list of duties 'named' in 247 CMR 8.00 and builds its first decision rule on that test; the regulations and the 247 CMR 2.00 definitions do not support it, and it contradicts the key to mapped question MA-Q-0075, so practice mapping fails. Second, it presents vaccine and medication administration as closed to every technician tier with no MA-versus-federal note, although the PREP Act COVID-19 Declaration (12th Amendment, 89 FR 99875) covers qualified pharmacy technicians administering COVID-19 and seasonal influenza vaccines and specified COVID-19 therapeutics through December 31, 2029 and treats contrary state law as preempted. Low items: the 8.08 exception, two refill-authorization cells stated as settled, direct supervision implied to be trainee-only, and the training-program topic requirement omitted. Targeted edits will cure it; a fresh audit is required.

findings.problem: The name-tag teaching says the tag follows 'what the Board has issued' and tells the candidate to 'Identify the credential the Board has issued to that individual and read the matching provision'. For the certified tier the Board issues only the pharmacy technician license; certified status comes from a Board-approved certifying body.
findings.rationale: Under 8.04(1)-(2) and the 247 CMR 2.00 definition, a certified pharmacy technician is a Board-registered pharmacy technician who is currently certified by a Board-approved certifying body. Applied literally, the decision rule sends a current certified technician to 8.02(6)(a) ('Pharmacy Technician') instead of 8.04(4)(a) ('Certified Pharmacy Technician'). comparison_tables[2] gets the tag right; the rule stated for applying it does not.

findings.problem: orientation[0] says the four credentialed categories 'are the whole of the counted population', and decision_logic[0] says to 'Count only' interns, certified technicians, technicians and trainees. Under 8.06(3)(b), persons outside the four definitions are excluded only as long as they are not supporting the pharmacist in any professional capacity, so they are counted once they do; the section's own worked_examples[1] counts such a cashier. orientation[0] also reduces the definitional limb to 'the credential the person holds', although the 247 CMR 2.00 definitions of pharmacy technician and trainee turn on performing pharmacy duties under direct supervision.
findings.rationale: The section's specific guidance (decision_logic[2], worked_examples[1], common_traps[3]) is correct, but its general counting rule contradicts it and would give the wrong count for an uncredentialed employee drawn into prescription work.

findings.problem: The resolution states flatly that 'the badges need the individual's first name', although the scenario's surname-only policy covers every badge and steps[1] correctly notes that 8.01(14) asks for the intern's name rather than a first name.
findings.rationale: The first-name rule belongs to the three technician provisions; the resolution extends it to the intern tier, contradicting the section's own step and comparison_tables[2].rows[0].

findings.problem: The section tells candidates to apply 'any narrower setting-specific Board policy' for an automated dispensing device or 'another specially regulated workflow' 'rather than the general 247 CMR 8.05 allocation', without identifying any policy, its content, or authority for a policy displacing 8.05.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.12 conditions automated dispensing device use on compliance with all laws, regulations and policies and on pharmacy policies covering stocking and controlled substances accountability; it does not displace 8.05. As written the entry names an exception without conveying its content and suggests 8.05 yields to an unidentified policy.

results.summary: Checked against 247 CMR 8.06(3), the four name-tag provisions, 247 CMR 8.05(1)-(3), 8.06(1)-(2) and 247 CMR 9.23(5)(a)-(d), and accurate on each: both ratios and all three routes to four; the 8.06(3)(b) exclusion and its proviso; the name and title on each tier's tag; transporting for the pharmacy technician versus transporting and handling for the certified technician, behind the written-policy proviso; the hydrocodone-only extended-release non-abuse-deterrent bar on all three technician grades with the express intern permission; production on request rather than advance filing; and the 30-day, five-day and 100-day absence thresholds with the substitute inventory performer. The hydrocodone-acetaminophen example matches 21 CFR 1308.12 and 1308.13. All eight mapped practice questions are answerable and consistent. Four Low defects prevent a KEEP: the tag rule is framed as following 'the credential the Board has issued', which misfits the certified tier; the general counting rule says to count only the four credentialed categories, contradicting the 8.06(3)(b) proviso and the section's own worked example; worked_examples[5] extends the first-name rule to interns; and exceptions[5] invokes an unidentified automated-dispensing 'Board policy' as displacing 8.05. Minor edits; a fresh audit is required.
